title: Community perceptions of socio-economic, environmental, and governance dimensions of manganese mining in Serenje District, Zambia.
abstract: Manganese has become increasingly important in the global energy transition, yet its extraction raises significant socio-economic, environmental, and governance concerns in mining-affected communities. This study examined community perceptions of the socio-economic benefits, environmental impacts, and governance dimensions of formal manganese mining in Serenje District, Zambia. Using a mixed-methods design, the study combined a household survey of 120 respondents across three communities with semi-structured interviews involving 14 purposively selected key informants, including company managers, industrial miners, traditional leaders, trade union representatives, and civil society stakeholders. Quantitative data were analysed using descriptive statistics and a Chi-Square test, while qualitative data were analysed thematically and interpreted alongside survey findings. The findings show that manganese mining is widely perceived as contributing positively to employment and local livelihoods, although key informants identified weak investment, poor infrastructure, ineffective policies, and market volatility as major constraints to long-term sector sustainability. Respondents also perceived notable environmental and health risks, particularly deterioration in water quality, biodiversity loss, respiratory problems, waterborne diseases, and skin conditions. Perceptions of Zambia's mining legal framework were mixed, with weak enforcement, outdated regulations, and limited institutional capacity identified as major governance concerns. Education level significantly influenced perceptions of mining's contribution to economic growth, while age and gender did not. The study contributes to resource governance and sustainable development debates by providing context-specific evidence on how mining is experienced and interpreted at the community level in an emerging manganese-producing district. It highlights the tension between perceived short-term socio-economic gains and longer-term environmental, health, and governance risks. The study recommends strengthening regulatory enforcement, improving institutional capacity, expanding environmental and public health monitoring, and adopting more inclusive mining policies that better reflect community experiences and priorities.
